utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are to call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I call Yevgeny Primakov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milosevic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Primakov.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will try to bear the limited time in mind so that you can finish with your testimony today, but I would like you to cover your biography very briefly, just main details from your biography, please.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Main details of my biography are as follows: I was elected to the Supreme Council of the USSR, and in 1998, I was elected to the upper chamber of our parliament, to the upper house. Following that, after the Soviet Union fell apart, towards late 1991 I was appointed the head of the central intelligence service. Following that, I was minister for foreign affairs. I served in that post for two years and eight months, and in 1998 and 1999, I was the Prime Minister of Russia, of the Russian Federation. Prior to that, prior to the Supreme Soviet, I was a journalist. I also was elected a member of the academy, Academy of Sciences of Russia, therefore I was an academician; and I was also head of two very significant scientific institutes: One was the Institute of Oriental Studies, and the other was the Institute of World Economy and International Relations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just check one thing. Can I take it your election to the upper house was in 1988?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prior to that, I was already a member of the Supreme Soviet, and I was elected to that body for the first time in 1988. In 1989, I was elected for the second time to the Supreme Soviet, and there I was the president of the upper chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, you participated actively and with significant influence in formulating Russian foreign policy throughout that decade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I participated in formulating Russian foreign policy in the 1990s, in view of my various posts. In that capacity, I took part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's what I thought. You were head of the intelligence service. You were minister of foreign affairs, and you were also the Prime Minister. So in those capacities, you covered foreign policy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout your work, when you dealt with the Balkans and Yugoslavia, were you involved in that directly?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes. I dealt with that directly in my official capacities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Starting in 1991, you became head of central intelligence service. Please tell us, what did the central intelligence service do in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Foreign intelligence service of Russia mostly dealt with the crisis in Yugoslavia, using its sources not only in the Balkans but also in other countries in order to create a full and complete picture of what was going on so that it could be reported to the leadership of the Russian Federation so that the Russian Federation could formulate a proper position in view of that situation. This was political intelligence activity, and with respect to that, I would like to tell you about the task that I was assigned by the head office. I have a text of this task assigned to me, in English, and I can turn this document over to the Chamber. In view of the expansion of NATO, the following telegram was sent: NATO alliance mission in Bosnia. In view of that mission, the task was set to us to establish to what extent the United States of America intends to involve Russia in the model of establishing security in Europe by using NATO mechanisms. We were mostly interested in the mechanisms allowing the Russian leadership to focus on the following issues: First of all: Is the practice relating to Bosnia and Herzegovina something that involves a purely local model, or is there a universal scenario in place allowing Washington to maintain and reinforce its position following the end of the Cold War? Second: What aspect of this model or scenario pertaining to allies of the USA pertains, and is the United States prepared to take into account those views which do not correspond to theirs? And third: What steps would be taken by the allies of the United States? And four: What is the situation concerning this in the United States itself? And the fifth: How does this relate to the expansion of NATO? Therefore, we had these five tasks that were sent to various departments, and I think this document shows just what level of interest existed within our agency, the intelligence agency, in view of the fact that we were interested in having a complete picture and informing our leadership about that. We wanted to know whether this was one single episode or whether this had a universal character, universal in a sense that after the end of the Cold War, there would be an attempt to create a European system of security through NATO mechanisms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what conclusion did you reach? Did this have a local or universal character?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: We came to the conclusion that what was going on was the formulation of a model aimed at using NATO mechanism outside of the territories of NATO Member States, and that in the future, United States will strengthen its efforts to use this mechanism outside of the NATO states, and the future confirmed that our conclusion was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There was no translation. Say that again, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked: What were your evaluations concerning the position of the West, the attitude of the West towards Belgrade? What characterised their attitude?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: This issue covers a number of years. I don't think that we immediately had the feeling that the West, and specifically the United States, would be so persistent and insistent in following the course of weakening Serbia. However, as time passed, it turned out exactly that way. For instance, I had meetings with the CIA chief, James Woolsey. During those meetings, we discussed Yugoslavia and the crisis in Yugoslavia, and to a certain extent we identified that even our two intelligence services looked exactly the same way upon a whole series of issues. I had a number of conversations with Mr. Woolsey, and I am prepared to hand over my notes to the Honourable Court. For instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, I'm stopping you. Mr. Milosevic, you must bring the witness to something that is closer -- to evidence that is closer to the issues in this case, otherwise questions of relevance will arise. I think the introductory part has gone far enough. Bring him to something that is more central, is more directly related to the issues Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond in the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can say very straightforwardly that from our point of view, in response to Mr. Milosevic's question, it is a fact that after a Democratic administration came to the White House it became evermore apparent that their course was to weaken Serbia, to not allow it to gain strength, and possibly even to complete the process of Yugoslavia's full disintegration. Are you happy with this answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You said that before. I want Mr. Milosevic to bring you to evidence that is closer to the issues that we are dealing with. Ask another question now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the political background of the West's attitude to the specific situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina which was your focus of attention?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Obviously one could also speak about humanitarian grounds. I'm not denying that. However, together with that, it is obvious that there was a political ground, political basis proceeding from the West's assumption that after Milosevic was unable, as leader of Serbia, to keep Yugoslavia together in its former shape, he placed his bets on the creation of the so-called Greater Serbia. That was the idea that our Western colleagues had. However, I absolutely don't share such view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this idea of a Greater Serbia had never featured in the plans of our state?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: In response to your question, I can refer, first of all, to my with you directly on the 8th of January, 1993. That was my first meeting with Mr. Milosevic, when I flew into Belgrade upon instructions from President Yeltsin following the submission at the Geneva conference of the Vance-Owen resolution on the 1st of January, and that plan envisaged an easing of tensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Within the framework of that discussion I had with Mr. Milosevic, he first agreed with my argument that in order to stabilise the situation in Bosnia, it is necessary to have a stable situation in Serbia. He also mentioned that the absence of a peaceful solution to the Bosnian crisis could lead to not only an external crisis for Serbia but also an internal one, because there were many hostile elements. When I asked him whether he nurtured any plans of a Greater Serbia, he said, emphatically, no. He said that this could be achieved only in theory, at the price of huge bloodshed. "And I'm not prepared to do that," he said. During that particular visit to Belgrade, the two of us agreed, and Milosevic specifically agreed, that he would go to Geneva and take part in the Geneva peace conference. At first he wasn't willing to go to Geneva, saying that it would be very difficult for him to do so against the background of such a violent, virulent anti-Serbian campaign in the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to address a question -- I want to address a question to you. In that meeting in Belgrade in January 1993, when you discussed with Mr. Milosevic the question of a Greater Serbia, what did you understand the -- that concept to mean? In practical terms, what did it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unification of all Serbs living in Yugoslavia into one state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't finish my previous answer. And then Mr. Milosevic travelled to Geneva. His conduct in Geneva confirms, as I see it, his chartered course of policy to stabilise Kosovo. He arrived in Geneva at a moment when the Republika Srpska authorities had already rejected the proposal of the constitution of the first article, the constitution of BH, and what was under discussion when he arrived was the territorial division in Bosnia. His further conduct confirmed, and further developments confirmed that he intended to accept the Vance-Owen resolution. And even when the situation in the Serbian Krajina grew much more tense vis-a-vis the Croats, he kept insisting on that. And when the parliament of Republika Srpska adopted the resolution rejecting the plan, rejecting agreement, everybody knows how Belgrade reacted. Belgrade practically imposed an economic blockade on Republika Srpska, allowing the passage of only humanitarian aid, qualifying it as the only possible position for anyone who had any responsibility. I watched the broadcast of Mr. Milosevic's speech in Geneva. He spoke of the two principles in the draft project of the future constitutional structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina. One, equality among all three ethnic communities and resolution of all issues by consensus. I believe this is clear testimony to the fact that he had no plans and conducted no actions to achieve a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Primakov, during this answer that at that time there was a virulent anti-Serbian campaign in the press. What were your thoughts and impressions from that time?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I remember one of the programmes that I saw on television that was shown in all Western countries in December, just before I arrived, and this programme showed a large group of people burying somebody. It was a funeral. And it was said that the people being buried were victims of Serbian genocide; however, in the procession at the funeral, you could see Orthodox priests. After that, apologies were made, and it was said that it was all a mix-up, that everything was exactly the other way around. However, it's my view that Serbs were being depicted as the aggressor side intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the general attitude of the Western media regarding the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I think I've already answered that question. The Western take was extremely negative. I mean, the whole attitude of the Western media. That is, I believe, common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From all that you know, because you are testifying, as we agreed, on the basis of your personal knowledge, can we take it that the Serbian side was responsible for the events in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Do you want to move on to Kosovo already, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will come back to certain topics yet, but I just wanted to ask you this question at precisely this point.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: You see, Kosovo, from my point of view, was a place that was seeing events testifying to the escalation of Albanian extremism and separatism. The initiators and the provocateurs of many events in Kosovo were the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army, which, by the way, was included by the US first into their list of terrorist organisations. With the intensification of the activities of that army, which thrived on volunteers and weapon supplies from Albania - and that became clearer and clearer after 1997 - followed by more reinforcements and weapon supplies from Europe, they started pushing back the Serbian army and the police, which retaliated and pushed them out of various villages. And the casualties in all that process were Albanian villagers. But the initiators of all that were the Kosovo Liberation Army. If you're asking me about the Western attitude to all that, I have already said that at the beginning this army was characterised as a terrorist organisation; however, later it was labelled almost as a mechanism for achieving liberty for the Albanian population, liberty and justice. I think the Western politicians, who took a long time to reach that conclusion, were led by Germany, which at that time worked hard to achieve the return to Kosovo of a large number of Albanians who had left Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Kosovo and who were working in Germany at the time. It was becoming a huge internal problem for Germany. And that is why the entire Western policy took that line towards the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Primakov. I wanted to single this out as a general question, but let us for the time being come back to the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tell me, what were you guided by? What were the underlying reasons for your conclusion that the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be dealt with by military means?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's not only my conclusion. His Honour the Judge did not allow me to read from the shorthand notes of my discussion with Mr. Woolsey, who at that time headed the CIA. It was also the conclusion of the CIA that there is no military solution to the BH crisis. And in effect, three ethnic communities were fighting each other, each defending its own interests, but in essence it was one and the same people, one and the same nation divided by ethnicity and religion. And it was impossible to deal with the problem militarily because that would inevitably damage the interests of one of the groups. It would dramatically damage the interests of either one group or, alternatively, the two other groups which wanted to unite, namely, the Croats and the Muslims, and opposed to them were the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, it is not the intention of the Chamber or the Judge not to allow you to read out the notes you made with the -- during the conversation with the CIA. The point was that Mr. Milosevic should put the specific questions to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the conversation you had with Mr. Woolsey, you have some shorthand notes, and you wanted to read them. If you believe that would complement your answer, add to it, please do so. And if you don't think that, then let's go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before -- Mr. Milosevic, we have been through this before. If he's going to read from notes, you must adduce from him evidence about the provenance of the notes; when they were made and the general context in which they were made.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I originally understood that Mr. Primakov had already explained that. He's talking about the notes of his discussion with his American colleague, Mr. Woolsey, that took place in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already emphasised a couple of points that can be derived from the notes of this discussion, and I don't intend to go back to it any more, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on, then. In your assessment and according to the data available to you then, what were the causes of the war no Bosnia-Herzegovina? What was the nature of that war?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: If you speak about the nature of that war, it was a civil war fed by external intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Primakov. Did the contacts that you said were successful when you spoke about your discussions with Mr. Woolsey continue? Did they continue?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not at the level that they had in 1993, that they had reached in 1993. They actually ceased, in the beginning of 1994, and we shifted to an exchange of information and only for a while. I believe that if the contacts had continued at the level where they were in 1993, and they included then visits by our representatives to Washington for negotiations about possible solutions to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I believe these talks were constructive, and if they had continued, if they had been able to continue, that would have had a very favourable effect on the policies and politics in all countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, I just want to explain to you that I'm waiting for the interpretation of your answer to finish, and this explains the brief pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I can see that, Mr. Milosevic. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, following this situation, you remember that on the eve of the elections in Serbia in December 1992, there was a NATO meeting in Brussels. Do you remember the kind of oratory that could be heard there?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: According to the information available to us at the time, criticism of Serbia gained force, and even appeals were heard from certain representatives to apply force against Serbia. Such statements became public, and in our view, that was an attempt to exert pressure generally, including on the forthcoming elections in Serbia and Montenegro. I believe that at that moment it was a demonstration of power aimed at achieving a political solution, a political outcome of the elections that would suit the West.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly -- or, rather, let me put it in the form of a question. Those positions taken in Brussels, were they just propaganda?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: It was both propaganda, but it was also the beginning of the implementation of a particular political course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was also the exertion of political pressure. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, you understand me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were aware of the position of Belgrade and my personal position?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, I was familiar with it, and I spoke about it already, about our first meeting in 1993, and I continued to be aware of your political position throughout many meetings we had after that. The quintessence of that position was that you didn't want to see any damage to the interests of Serbs in the conflict that was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and I felt that at the same time you wanted a peaceful solution which is a reflection of your later stance at the Dayton negotiations. I didn't participate in the Dayton negotiations, but I had a conversation with a colleague when I was already foreign minister. I spoke to the US state secretary, Madeleine Albright, and asked her this question: "Do you believe that in Dayton you could achieve success in stabilising the situation in Bosnia were it not for the role played by Milosevic?" And she answered unequivocally, "No. Without Milosevic, we could not achieve a positive outcome."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did Russia assess, and what attitude did Russia take with respect to our position and our efforts to achieve a peaceful settlement in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Russia unequivocally held onto the position that it was necessary to establish stabilisation and to avoid bloodshed in Bosnia-Herzegovina and it achieve political settlement in that country, and everything that was done in order to achieve that by Mr. Milosevic was that Russia supported, providing that it was done within those principles that Russia abided by. In view of that, I would like to say that after my first meeting with Mr. Milosevic, pursuant to the directive issued by President Yeltsin, on the 14th of January, a representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was told to convey to Mr. Milosevic that the president of Russia had a favourable view concerning his efforts on achieving peaceful settlement in Bosnia, and he issued an order to our agencies to take measures aimed at ensuring the change of position towards Belgrade that existed within certain countries, Islamic countries included. That would favour the achievement of peaceful settlement in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was the statement of our government that was conveyed to the representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who was told to convey this to President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I observe that the witness periodically reads from pieces of paper in a file he has. On one occasion it appeared Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond to have been a note or something. On other occasions it may simply be preparations for the giving of testimony. It maybe helpful if we know what he is reading from from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Primakov, you've heard the point made by the Prosecutor. You're not to read from any note unless it has been brought to the Court's attention before and has received the approval of the Court. So let us know when you're reading from a particular note, and we'll ask you about the circumstances in which the note was made and then determine whether to allow you to read from it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I simply wish to say that this instruction is something that I conveyed to Mr. Milosevic through our representative, and I did it pursuant to the instructions I had received from President Yeltsin. Your Honour, I do not believe that this is a document that can be presented in the courtroom. This is a document that goes through coded communications. It's a coded telegram, and it would be difficult to present it here as evidence. If I was invited here to give evidence, if I was invited here to come as a witness, and as you know, I was head of the foreign intelligence service, I was a minister of foreign affairs, and I was Prime Minister of Russia; therefore, I think that a Court should have a certain amount of trust to what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, trust is one matter, Mr. Primakov, but we have rules of evidence that we must abide by, and in future, whenever you're going to read from a note, from a book, that must be brought to the attention of the Court before. And, Mr. Milosevic, you must bear that in mind. And you should know this by now. We've been through that before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you were able to see for yourself that Mr. Primakov read out from the instructions sent by the service concerning the issues of NATO views and so on. Therefore, he read out from his own documents, from the instruction that he had received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's not the point. The point is that we must know what he's reading from. The general rule is that evidence must come from his mouth. If he is reading from a note that he has made, the Court must know that. The Prosecutor may want to cross-examine on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Primakov --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me clarify one thing. Mr. Primakov, was the document that you read from an original -- is it interpretation or -- excuse me. Is it a note you made for the preparation of this evidence, or is it the note or translation of coded document to be presented to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is verbatim instruction that I passed on to our representative so that the view of Russia concerning the travel of Mr. Milosevic to Geneva can be made known and so that this could be conveyed to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you are not in position to hand the document over to the Court, or are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you are probably aware of, Your Honour, these documents are not proper documents. These are coded telegrams, and no state would make known the system of its coded telegrams, even after many years have passed. So this is what I passed on to our representative in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, you quoted verbatim what you passed on, the information that you passed on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's follow on on this. Do you remember our meeting which took place in Belgrade two months after the initial meeting?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that meeting well. I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This meeting, did it give any further contribution to the efforts to reach a peaceful settlement?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: During that meeting, you confirmed once again your intention to abide by the course proposed in the resolution of Vance-Owen Plan, and that was the main issue, as far as I could tell, discussed at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now let us turn to Kosovo. I put only one general question to you concerning Kosovo that had to do with responsibility, and you gave me your answer about separatist and terrorist activity. My question is as follows: Did the Russian side know about the preparations of terrorists and their activities undertaken in that province; and to what extent was Russia informed about that?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: We were informed about the events taking place. We were informed about the fact and that there were reinforcements of soldiers coming in from Albania. However, I have to say that Albania itself did not start supporting separatism in Kosovo from the beginning. In 1996, at the General Assembly, I had a meeting with the minister of foreign affairs of Albania, who told me that Albanian policy meant that Kosovo should be seen as part of Yugoslavia. And this was something that I, as minister of foreign affairs at the time, supported very firmly. However, the position changed later on in view of what was happening in Albania itself at the time. There was disorder and chaos in that country at the time, and the forces that supported the KLA gained in influence and force at the time. This was well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The position of Albania is something that you have explained. Did you discuss the issue of Kosovo with the Western leaders?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: There was a discussion with Western leaders at practically all meetings of the Contact Group, the ones that I took part in as minister of foreign affairs. I believe that several such meetings could be named here, the meetings that testify that there was a confrontation of opinions there, occasionally leading to disputes, because it was obvious what was going on in Kosovo. I took part in the Contact Group meeting for the first time on the 24th of September, 1997. I'm not reading out from a document, I'm reading from my note. Am I allowed to do that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did you make those notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made these notes yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may read from them briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not reading out, I'm just looking at the text. I'm not reading out from the text. So on the 24th of September, 1997, the first meeting of the Contact Group in which I participated took place, and at the time, at the proposal of Klaus Kinkel, a German foreign minister, at his firm proposal, the first statement of the Contact Group was adopted. And as is well known, this statement did not deal with Kosovo or Bosnia-Herzegovina. This statement was formulated back at the time when Yugoslavia disintegrated and when various conflicts erupted. Then the first statement was adopted concerning Kosovo, and I believe that it was a balanced statement. The text was carefully formulated, and the text acknowledged that this was an internal conflict, and the text expressed concern with the fact that the situation was not regulated. At the end of February 1998, the situation in Kosovo became more tense, and in that background, another meeting was held, a meeting of the Contact Group in London on the 8th of March. I also took part in that meeting. And at the time, United States and UK proposed that economic sanctions be imposed against Yugoslavia. We attempted to ensure that these sanctions apply only to supply of weapons to Yugoslavia. This was confirmed by the Western colleagues that this did not pertain only to Yugoslavia, meaning not only to Serbia, but to Kosovo as well. I think that another meeting that ought to be mentioned here is a meeting of Contact Group in Bonn on the 25th of March, held at the level Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond of the ministers of foreign affairs. There were significant disagreements expressed there. The main role was played, naturally, by the Americans there. The position taken there did not suit us because it wasn't a balanced position and did not reflect the objective reality. And when I failed to give my consent to that text, Kinkel showed himself to be a very wise politician, and he managed to reach a consensus and to iron out the disagreements, and then the final text was fairly balanced. At the following meeting, a package of stabilisation measures was taken, and at that meeting there was condemnation of Albanian terrorists expressed. I can also give you other information stemming from Contact Group meetings which confirm that the Western side wanted to increase its pressure on Serbia, on Yugoslavia, through a system of economic measures, economic sanctions, which is something that we disagreed with. We formulated our opinion, the essence of which was that we were against the freezing of assets, and we were against the ban on new investment in Yugoslavia. This was our position that was expressed, and in order not to sabotage the entire effort, we did adopt these resolutions which, in our mind, gave a more balanced note to the entire effort thanks to our contribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In future your answers should be shorter. Mr. Milosevic, direct more questions to the witness. The Court doesn't profit from answers which are so long.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, precisely in order to save time, I believe that these efforts with the Contact Group are such that I would not have put a question to Mr. Primakov about the meeting of Contact Group in Bonn and London and so on. I wasn't going to deal with each of these meetings individually, because that would have taken up a lot of time. As it stands, he described these meetings very briefly, gave a conclusion about each of these meetings, expressing that there was serious pressure exerted upon Yugoslavia. My question to Mr. Primakov is as follows:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, were the efforts of the Contact Group something that fed separatism from outside? Are the efforts of Contact Group something that fed pressures from outside?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that statement that the efforts of Contact Group fed separatism from outside. However, there were some episodes that did feed the separatism from outside, and I will give you two such episodes. The first one was depicting KLA fighters as someone who was fighting for justice, and the second instance were the efforts of our Western partners to avoid at any cost the mentioning of the fact that Kosovo issue needs to be resolved within the framework of Serbia. At any cost, avoiding the mentioning of that. They spoke of Yugoslavia without mentioning Serbia, and this is where we and others could see that they were attempting to introduce a partial solution, an interim solution which would lead to the separation of Kosovo. They were, in fact, attempting to turn Kosovo into another Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Well, did this fact feed the separatism from outside?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, it did feed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Mr. Primakov mentioned these two moments, these two instances, namely that KLA terrorists were depicted as justice fighters, and the other one that there was an attempt to avoid mentioning this within the framework of Serbia, I received the translation that Mr. Primakov used the term "episode." He didn't say "episode."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. You're raising a translation point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. In the translation, the interpretation, I heard that Mr. Primakov described this as an episode. He didn't use the term "episode." He described this as two factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did you say, Mr. Primakov?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not the episode but the interaction, the activity that existed within the Contact Group which objectively stirred up or fed separatism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into details, but can you please tell me what took place in Bonn during the Contact Group meeting at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: If you're interested in the entourage issues, I can tell you that when Klaus Kinkel invited me into his office and we started negotiating various formulations, behind the window there was a demonstration of Albanians going on. Kinkel told me, "Do you see under what kind of pressure I have to work?" And I responded to him, "Why don't you announce that you will put down the -- put down the names of all those taking part in the demonstrations, and there will be nobody there any more," because all those taking part in the demonstrations definitely did not want to go back to Kosovo. And this was confirmed by events later on, because all of them remained living in Germany, because Germany has a much higher living standard than Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to Contact Group ministers, you also discussed Kosovo with your American counterpart, Vice-president Al Gore.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us only those details which pertain to your conversation and how you viewed the refugees from Kosovo and Metohija and how he viewed them. What was his position about refugees from Kosovo and Metohija, and what was your position regarding them?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: This conversation took place on the eve of -- or, rather, after the airstrikes had started, after they had started. That was not the first conversation I had with Mr. Gore. Gore claimed that millions of refugees were leaving Kosovo, Albanian refugees, travelling through mountains, suffering greatly, and that that was precisely the reason for the airstrikes. I told him that according to our information, the wave of refugees reached its greatest level precisely after the beginning of airstrikes, and immediately said that he, mildly speaking, was exaggerating because there could not be 1 million refugees in Kosovo in view of its entire population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify something, Mr. Primakov. If I understood you well, you are saying that the reason people became refugees was bombing, the airstrikes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Not quite. Naturally, people became refugees for other reasons as well, but these great numbers, these vast numbers, and this wide-scale process, this wide-scale process, according to our information, started after the airstrikes had begun. And this was something that was acknowledged by refugees themselves, refugees who gave public statements. They explained their departure by the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me very briefly, how did Russia view the arms embargo?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I already said, Mr. Milosevic, that we viewed this measure as the necessity to refrain from arms deliveries not only to Yugoslavia but also to Kosovo where it could be used and abused by separatists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's time for the adjournment. Mr. Primakov, we're going to take an adjournment now. Judge Bonomy wants to ask a question before we take the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, near the beginning of your evidence you referred to two documents. One was a telegram, I think, that had been circulated to sources that you had in various countries, and the other was notes you made of your meeting with Woolsey, and you gave the impression that these were documents you could produce to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You are right, Your Honour. I could submit them to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to know. That's all I wanted to know. It's a matter for Mr. Milosevic to decide whether he wishes them to be produced. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, what was the position of the state secretary, Madeleine Albright, in Bonn on the 25th of March at the ministerial meeting?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, Mrs. Albright, who represented the United States at the Contact Group meeting, insisted on the adoption of a resolution which stepped up pressure upon Belgrade. It was a resolution that envisaged the taking of forcible measures, measures of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was your stance, then?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I have already said that our position boiled down to a rejection of a one-sided reaction to Kosovo events, even more so because the possibilities for a political settlement were far from exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the danger then appear of Russia walking out of the Contact Group?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. During the session of the Contact Group, when I felt that such a resolution was being pushed, I said that in case it is adopted, I would no longer be willing to be among the participants supporting it, and I was prepared to walk out. After that, Kinkel invited me to his office and instructed his deputy, Ischinger, to find some language, some wording that would satisfy all the members of the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you then realise that your partners in the Contact Group were ultimately ready to use force against Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that because we already had information about ongoing preparations for implementing one of the options on NATO's table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You and I met as early as the 11th of March, 1998, and had a long conversation. Were you happy with the outcome of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: In principle, I was happy with the results of that meeting because the next day Milutinovic, who was at that time president of Serbia, made a statement saying that Serbia was ready and willing to start negotiating with Rugova. That was the main point of our discussion. And for the main part, it was the answer that we were seeking from you. The fact that it was not you who made the statement but Mr. Milutinovic was something that I didn't understand at the outset, but I later understood that it is explained by the fact that it was Serbia who was dealing with Kosovo, and he was the President of Serbia, not you. You were president of Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused proposed this meeting as being on the 11th of March. It may be that he and the witness may want to review, for purposes of getting the record straight, whether it's the 11th or possibly the 17th. It may be the translation I've got of a document's wrong, but it may be worth checking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 17th of March, 1998. That was when the meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, was it a fact that tensions were easing on Kosovo and the situation was going back to normal?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I cannot say that normalcy had already been restored. However, after the statement of Mr. Milutinovic, there was a certain easing of tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in mid-May discussions were started with Rugova?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes. That is a known fact. It was a known fact that discussions with Rugova had started, and representatives of both parties had begun meeting in Pristina. However, a week later, something happened as a result of which the negotiations broke down. The initiator of those events was the KLA, who cut off the major thoroughfare linking Serbia with Kosovo. The KLA infiltrated the border areas with Albania and established themselves there, setting up checkpoints. As a result, Serbian forces were activated, and clashes began taking a toll on the civilian population. That is why the negotiations broke down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After that, was there another easing of tensions and a tendency towards normalisation?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Throughout the time, there were two parallel tracks. One reflected objective events and the possibilities for a peaceful settlement. It was displayed in a whole number of ways. On the other hand, it is a fact that Western governments were taking an ever more rigid stance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly, although the situation was improving and calming down, the pressure on Belgrade increased? Is that so? Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: In principle you did understand me correctly, because for instance, on the 6th of July, 1998, the international diplomatic observers mission started its work. The Contact Group was at the time discussing the status of Kosovo. The presence of Mr. Hill, ambassador of the USA, was notable there. On the 13th of August, he announced negotiations with the Kosovo Albanians. And there was my assistant together with him, Mr. Afanas'ievskii, and things looked as if they were moving towards a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, Mr. Robinson, it is Mr. Afanas'ievskii. His name was not properly recorded or pronounced by interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, we are now coming to my visit to Moscow in June 1998. Please briefly describe what happened, what we discussed, you, President Yeltsin, and myself in Moscow in June 1998. What was the outcome of that meeting, and what were its consequences?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: You were invited to come to Moscow for negotiations with President Yeltsin first, and then you discussed with myself, the defence minister and his colleagues the elaboration of a joint statement, joint communique that was to include several general points; namely, your readiness to allow the refugees to return, your readiness to cooperate with the High Commissioner for Refugees of the UN and the International Red Cross, also the possibility of a visit to Kosovo by international organisations, your intention to start negotiations that would include, on the Serbian side, representatives of the Serb population of Kosovo as well as Albanian representatives, and Rugova also on the Albanian side. We came to a stalemate of sorts discussing the special purpose forces of Serbia and their withdrawal from Kosovo. You explained that it was impossible to effect such a one-sided measure by saying that if it happens, then the Serbian population would start to flee Kosovo and a genocide against Serbs would start. That's why you were not prepared to go forward with it. That was recorded in the joint statement. You undertook to effect a withdrawal of the army in exchange for a cessation of hostilities on the part of the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That document exists. It was said in exchange here. It was not exactly said that way. It was said that the army would withdraw in the measure of or insofar as a cessation of hostilities would be effected.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: There was a proportionality instituted between the two processes, the withdrawal of the Yugoslav army from Kosovo and the cessation of hostilities by Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That agreement and the substance of that joint statement, was that honoured by our side?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: It was honoured and implemented, and I believe that some events, some further developments in Kosovo and around it confirmed that it was possible to finalise a political settlement. In addition to what I already said in response to your previous question, I would like to emphasise and draw everybody's attention to the fact that the current president of OSCE and the foreign minister of Yugoslavia, Jovanovic, signed an agreement to set up an OSCE Verification Mission for Kosovo. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond And on the 15th of October, an agreement was signed between the Republic of Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and NATO about air surveillance over the situation in Kosovo. By 24th October, a UN Security Council resolution was passed to follow up on this agreement, and it was precisely at that moment that we saw an insisting stance, position, in the United Nations to go forward with a more firm approach, a hard-line approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a follow-up, I have another question. Were there any suggestions and proposals or influence exerted for a UN resolution to be passed based on Chapter VII?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes. It was precisely at that time that our Western partners took a turn towards passing a hard line-resolution in the UN Security Council including the invocation of Chapter VII of the Statute, which envisages a possibility of escalating activities up to use of force against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the position of Russia? What was your position?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: On this issue, I can say that Russia was pressured to some extent to agree to this viewpoint. And to corroborate that, I can tell you about a telephone conversation I had with Klaus Kinkel, with whom I had a friendly relationship. And he even sent me a letter about that through his representative with whom I met in Sochi where I was at the time. And in this letter he insisted that Russia should agree with this approach. And even despite our friendly relationship, there was an aftertaste of threat in that letter in the event of Russia's failure to agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you answer?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I answered that from my point of view, political means were far from exhausted, that we should seek political agreement, and that in our eyes the invocation of Chapter VII was inadmissible because we thought it could open the door to military action and use of force against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had a negative attitude to any kind of operation against Yugoslavia; to the separation of Kosovo from Yugoslavia, to the escalation of sanctions against Yugoslavia. Would that correctly describe Russia's stance on the Yugoslav issue at the time?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: You quite correctly described Russia's position at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Primakov. And what was the situation in the UN Security Council?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: The issue was being debated. There was a polemic, fruitless, as I believe, because the resolution was not passed as it would have approved military action against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Primakov, did we in Belgrade do anything to provoke NATO's airstrikes against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Well, you see, I would distinguish between two aspects. I believe there was no firm, streamlined policy on the part of Yugoslavia of that kind. However, there were certain excesses that could support the argument that this vicious circle of violence was not interrupted. At the same time, both according to our information and from what I know from my conversations with you, I observed that both you personally and Belgrade were trying to rein in the forces that could be drawn into that circle of violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on now. Are you aware of the position of the Yugoslav delegation in Rambouillet negotiations in February and March 1999?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that position. At the time, I had already become the Prime Minister of Russia, and of course it could not have passed me by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was Yugoslavia given an ultimatum regarding Kosovo in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Undisputedly, the demand to accept a resolution in Rambouillet was given in the form of an ultimatum. I must say that from our point of view, the resolution was, on the whole, acceptable for Yugoslavia, but at the same time there was one issue on which the Yugoslavs would not agree with that resolution. This was the demand for an international military presence in Kosovo. And because of this word "military," the whole thing exploded, because behind it there was the obvious intent of NATO to bring its forces to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly as saying that, in your opinion, the real objective of the Rambouillet agreement was to allow the deployment of NATO forces in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Primakov. Could you now answer this question: What were the objectives of your mission to Belgrade on the 30th of March, 1999, six days after the start of the bombing of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I travelled to Belgrade as I was asked to do directly by the French president, Chirac, who called me and asked me to fly to Belgrade in order to receive, as he put it, "sufficient signals from Mr. Milosevic in order to stop the bombing." When I asked Chirac on the telephone what kind of signals would they have to be, he answered, "At least a small signal." I asked, "Do you mean at least in the framework of the Contact Group?" He said, "Well, at least." So I went to Belgrade, and in Belgrade I talked to Mr. Milosevic, and in our understanding, we did receive that signal. However, according to the initial idea given to us by President Chirac, that meant guarantees of return of refugees, cessation of hostilities, start of negotiations, international monitoring. And with this set of issues, we were to fly to Bonn and hand it all over to the federal Chancellor Schroeder who was, at that time, president of the European Union. However barely had our plane taken off that the bombing of the airport started. And the West had no idea at that time what we had in our hands at the moment, and that was the end of this attempt to obtain this signal. But I would like to add one more detail, with your leave, Your Honour. When this discussion in Belgrade took place, Mr. Milosevic told me, while we talked, "I'm ready to withdraw all of my forces from Kosovo if NATO forces withdraw from the border of Macedonia." And this was the first mention of this second condition, second interlinkage that could have been of use, that could have been of some service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, they never had any intention of even hearing you out on the outcome of your discussions with me.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: When we arrived in Bonn, I, too, gained the impression that the response to our proposal to stop the airstrikes was predetermined, our proposal being based on receiving such signals from Mr. Milosevic. And I had that impression that it was predetermined because we had never had the chance to even tell what we had achieved to the federal Chancellor. He never had the chance to tell us that it was not enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Court has taken note of the wish of this witness to return today, and indeed you had indicated that. We have made an arrangement which would allow us to sit until 2.30. In order to achieve some measure of equality and fairness in terms of the cross-examination, it would seem, then, that it would be -- you would finish your examination-in-chief by about 10.50, if that is -- 11.50, rather, if that is possible, and we would then sit from -- we will take a break at 12.20. We will break for 30 minutes, return at 12.50 and then break at 2.30. It's a matter for you to decide, but that is the arrangement which we can make if the witness is to return today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Prosecution will be given two hours, and then you will be given an extra ten minutes for re-examination. In total, you have about two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I entirely agree. I will honour the deadlines, and I did not even expect it to be this generous. I have to admit that. I definitely wanted to conclude with the examination today so that Mr. Primakov could attend to his other duties. I hope to even take less time than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Primakov, therefore they did not even display readiness to hear you out concerning the results of your visit to Belgrade. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: You see, nobody interrupted me there, naturally. We had very good relations, Chancellor Schroeder and I and others. However, as I expressed the points that we identified or formulated during the conversation with you in Belgrade, Schroeder immediately said, "This is insufficient" without listening to supplemental explanations of those points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Based on your experience, you as Russian Prime Minister at the time spoke to other leaders. Were there any other leaders who held a negative view concerning the air raids of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I can quote the words of federal Chancellor Kohl who, in retrospect assessing the situation, said that it was an historic mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation well. Did you say that Chancellor Kohl said that an historic mistake had been made? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this historic mistake was the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Primakov. Please tell me, you, Russian government, Russian leadership, how did all of you view the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia, which was done without prior consent of the UN Security Council, and how did you see what repercussions it had on the international order and the interests of various nations, including Russia?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Russia took a very negative approach with respect to the bombing, and this was widely known. We used all of our contacts. I personally spoke about it with President Chirac, with D'Alema, who was the Italian Prime Minister at the time, and with the US vice-president, Al Gore, urging them to at least make a pause in the bombing, or better yet, to immediately cease with the bombing. I knew that similar conversations were conducted with President Yeltsin and his counterparts. However, there was nothing we could do about it, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how do you view this NATO action undertaken without the UN Security Council consent with respect or in relation to the interests of the international community?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't ask the witness questions which you know are a matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will reformulate the question. I have in mind that here in the witness stand we have Russian Prime Minister who was Prime Minister at the time. Therefore, he's undoubtedly competent to give us his position. All right. I will reformulate my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were the general consequences, in view of the international community, of the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I think that this has opened the door for ignoring the necessity of obtaining a consent prior to taking action against certain states. This undermines, undoubtedly, the international order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, I have cut you off. I have cut you off. Mr. Milosevic, a trend is developing in your examination-in-chief. In your desire to end your examination-in-chief on a kind of flourish, you tend to overstep evidential bounds. If you have nothing more to ask the witness that is within the bounds of the Rules, you should stop and allow the cross-examination to begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have other questions. I do, Mr. Robinson, not to worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, in your view, did the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia contribute to finding a solution to the Kosovo crisis?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: The Kosovo reality tells us that the problem of Kosovo is far from being resolved. The Serb population has practically deserted Kosovo. Therefore, this problem is far from solved. And I think that the bombing did not help regulate the situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the activity of Albanian terrorists continues to this day in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not allowing that. Don't answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, the entire international media wrote extensively about the U-turn that you made over the Atlantic Ocean. Can you tell us, what was that about?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Being Prime Minister, I was on my way to the United States where I was supposed to have meetings mostly dealing with the economic relations between Russia and the United States, and this was within the framework of the Gore-Primakov commission. Prior to that there used to be a Gore-Chernomyrdin commission. When we landed in Shannon, this was an interim landing, I learned that, as I was told by our ambassador in Washington, the decision to bomb was 98 per cent ready. I called Vice-president Gore and asked him to inform me of the developments of the events, stressing that we valued our relations with the United States and that because of that I would continue my trip to the United States. However, while on board in the air, I contacted Gore once again, and he told me that the decision was practically adopted. Under those circumstances, I believed that it was impossible for me to continue with my visit to the United States, and therefore my plane made a U-turn in midair, and we flew back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Another question, Mr. Primakov. We had General Ivasov testifying here. He claims that NATO bombing was the cause of the fact that refugees left Kosovo. And in addition to that, he said that NATO had been planning an action in Kosovo from at least from mid-1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the form of the question is, I think, inappropriate and inadmissible. I don't mind if the witness answers it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the specific question, Mr. Milosevic? What is the specific question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think I'm speaking rather slowly because of the interpreters, so what I said was that General Ivasov testified here, and that he claimed two things: One, that the NATO bombing was the cause of massive exodus, and that the war against Yugoslavia had been planned a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Can you confirm these claims, or will you deny them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, although I believe you've already spoken on that issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the first issue, yes, I voiced my opinion. As for the second part of your opinion -- of your question, Mr. Milosevic, I believe that General Ivasov, in view of the post he held with the General Staff, had a right to make up his opinion, including, among other things, classified sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Primakov.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, I've got several topics to deal with, and I'll try and deal with them in an orderly way. Just by way of opening observations or questions, there are one or two things you said. You spoke of the Democratic administration in the United States being determined either to weaken Serbia or not to allow it to gain strength. Why should Serbia be allowed to gain strength vis-a-vis other component parts of the former Yugoslavia, please?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: At the time, especially within the Democratic party which came to power and came to the White House, an ideological position with respect to Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Mr. Milosevic was formulated, and therefore there was this geopolitical view that Milosevic attempted to prevent the breaking apart of Yugoslavia, and that was not in accordance with the US plans. They realised that the centre of the country was Serbia, which was the only place where the Socialist Party was still in power, the Socialist Party headed by Mr. Milosevic. And that party was the successor of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. And as I saw it, this is why their position with respect to Mr. Milosevic was an extremely ideological one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The question I asked was not, of course, why they should favour a weakening of Serbia but why anybody should favour a strengthening of Serbia vis-a-vis the other component parts of Yugoslavia, and I don't think you've answered that specific question which arises from your answer.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I think that I did answer your question. Precisely because they thought -- they in the West thought that Serbia was the basis of the remaining communism in Yugoslavia. Therefore, they tried to weaken Yugoslavia. And Milosevic who was at the helm of Serbia at the time was not an acceptable figure for them. This is the position up until Dayton. Then during Dayton and after Dayton, the West changed its position to a certain degree and then went back to the initial position. Nobody said that they should have strengthened Serbia, but they shouldn't have weakened it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can we look, please, at a couple of extracts from your book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there will be, with this witness and with other witnesses, occasions when it will be helpful to ask them about particular passages in books that they've written or indeed in books that others have written on the topics of which they speak. It seems to me preferable, to avoid suggestions of taking things out of context, that we either print whole chapters of books, even if we only go to extracts from them, so that the chapters can be available. And with this witness, there are two chapters from his book, Years in Big Politics, that I have printed -- or had printed and translated, although there are only very limited references that I'm going to make to the first of the two parts that you have. What you have at the moment is, I hope -- would Your Honours just give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is the Russian version of the author before him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, I've provided you with a copy of the book that you wrote, or parts of it, in any event. I only want your help at the moment with one point. You spoke of the meeting that you had with the accused on the 8th of January of 1993. You were asked a question by the accused about Greater Serbia, and your answer was that the accused said that that could only be achieved at the cost of great bloodshed. Now, in giving your answer to the Court today, had you referred to any notes?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Not only at the cost of great bloodshed, but he also added that because of that, that course was unacceptable. Please quote my answers as I've given them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, I do my best with the handwriting that's available to me, and you're always free to correct me. In order to give that account to the Judges, had you refreshed your memory from any contemporaneous notes?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Everything is fresh in my memory. I can recollect everything without notes. However, I do have some notes. As for my book, I find it a great pleasure that you have read it. However, you shouldn't have bothered translating it, because the book has already been translated into many languages and has been published in practically all countries throughout the world. I want to say, I want to make sure that this goes into the record, that all facts mentioned in my book, both in the first one and the second one, received no criticism from my Western colleagues. So there was not a single objection claiming that I portrayed something inaccurately. I'm just saying this to illustrate how well I remembered the conversations I had with my counterparts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Primakov, two things: In order to enable you to leave today, we have to go for slightly shorter answers, with your leave. And the second thing is, I'm indeed grateful for the book and its accuracy, because the suggestion of a date being the 11th of March was one that I was able to correct from your book to the 17th of March, of 1998. Would you now perhaps be good enough to go to page 176 of the Russian text and page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I apologise, what page in Russian?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 176 I'm advised.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Had I known this, I would have brought my own copy. 173?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And we're now looking at the account that you give of the discussion with the accused in that first meeting of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice says page 76 in English. My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 6 in English and 176 in Russian, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, when we look at the book, Mr. Primakov, and the way you summarise the account there, you say this: "The conversation then moved on to the plans for a Greater Serbia. I emphasised that in the current conditions these were utterly unachievable, even at the cost of much blood spilled. Milosevic agreed with this." Over the page in the English. "I told Milosevic that whether someone wanted this or not, that was the reality. He was a key figure and the course of events throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, particularly --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the thinner version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand. Where do you see a contradiction, Mr. Nice, between what I said and what is stated in the book? Could you please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, if your account in the book is accurate, then you moved on to the plans for a Greater Serbia, apparently discussing them rather generally, and then it was you who emphasised that they were unachievable, even at the cost of blood, and it was the accused who agreed with you, not he raising it as his idea. Now, please, is that correct? Did you have to say to him, "Greater Serbia's out. It's going to be too expensive in blood"?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Isn't it sufficient that I mention in the book that we discussed this topic and both of us reached the same conclusion? Mr. Milosevic confirmed the same thing to me. That's what I mention here. I don't see any contradiction here. I don't see a discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Despite how hard I try to find a discrepancy, I don't see one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You spoke of a second meeting in March of 1993. This is on page 9 of the English version, and it will be on page 177, I'm advised, in the Russian. In your book, you say this: "I believe that his support for this line which served a peaceful outcome to the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the interests of all three communities was facilitated by a second, closed meeting in Belgrade with President Milosevic in March 1993." And then you go on to explain how you will describe other open meetings later. This closed meeting involved you and the accused and Mr. Stanisic? Was he present at this meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: It is possible that he attended the general part of the meeting, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond but my meeting with Mr. Milosevic was tete-a-tete. I don't think that this gentleman attended all meetings, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Am I right - just help me - that it was at this meeting in March of 1993 that special close communications were set up between the intelligence services of Russia and the intelligence services of the former Yugoslavia, with Mr. Stanisic being something of the link; correct?
