utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: No. He was not the link. He headed Serbian intelligence service. Yes, I did meet with him. He was an interlocutor, and I did meet with him when I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this meeting, described as a close meeting, was this the meeting where the close intelligence connection was forged or established?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: No. The links between intelligence services were started during my first visit to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is another passage of the book which I'll turn to later when we get to the Kosovo section. As His Honour Judge Kwon has correctly identified, one is slim and the other is a little larger. I'm happy for them to be both exhibited, if that's the Court's desire, now for good order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be exhibited now. Numbers please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the slim one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the slim one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They're both of them from the same book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They come from the same book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Different chapters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So they can -- they can both be from the same book, maybe both the same exhibit number

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So tab 1 for the thin one and tab 2 for the thick one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With that visit of the 8th of January in mind, Mr. Primakov, and your account of the accused's response in it, do you accept that by the end of December 1992, Serbs held some 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia despite being only some 30-odd per cent of the population?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: At the time when the military operation was already under way, the Serbs did indeed control practically 70 per cent of the territory, but I wish to draw your attention, Mr. Nice, to another fact. Pursuant to the Vance-Owen proposal, the Serbs were given, at their own request, over a half of the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Hardly surprising, was it, that the accused would favour the plan, as you explain he did; correct?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: That plan included not only territorial divisions, Mr. Nice. If you are really familiar with the plan, Mr. Nice, it also included the main point, and that is the constitutional order of the new state that was to deal with the status of those three ethnic communities. That plan opened the door to a stabilisation of the overall situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Serb-held territories in Croatia were on hold under the status quo for the time being; correct?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Serb-held territories in Croatia were still held by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: At the moment when the fighting was still going on there, then certainly each side occupied certain territories that could have included possibly population of the other side. But it was precisely that plan that envisaged final territorial divisions to enable stabilisation with a view to creating a structure in the future capable of preserving peace between the three communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, at the time of your meeting on the 8th of January of 1993, the accused, on behalf of Serbs, could hardly have got more than he had already achieved or than had already been achieved for Serbs on the ground. Isn't this correct?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: You will have to excuse me, Mr. Nice, but I don't understand the logic behind your question. If the accused, as you call him, accepts the plan which obviously reduces the territory held by Serbs from 70 per cent, as you yourself said, to 50 per cent, then where do you see his fault?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to what happened in a minute, but just confirm for me, please, good though your intelligence links with the -- with Serbia and with the former Yugoslavia may have been, you didn't have access, did you, to records of their innermost cabinet meetings or their innermost council meetings, did you?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Meetings between who and who? What records do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, for example, there was something called the Council for Harmonisation or the Council for Reconciliation on the Stands of State Politics. It's slightly different titles, but it was a body which had the accused and other top politicians from the former Yugoslavia, along with such people as General Mladic and other leading military figures, and that was meeting at about this time and indeed met on the day following your encounter with the accused on the 8th of January. You, I take it, would never have had access to the records of such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I think that not only I didn't have access to the classified documents of the Yugoslav side, nobody had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: If, if you want to familiarise me with it, it would be very useful. But then I would appreciate it if you would also tell me the provenance of these documents, just as you're asking me about mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov --

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Where do they come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, you shall have all of these questions answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Nice wishes to ask him, like he mentioned now this Council for the Harmonisation of Views, then it would be important to explain whose council it was, whether it was a council of Yugoslavia, because Serbia did not have one. Yugoslavia only had one. He should say who chaired the council, who summoned or convened the meetings. I could have been only one of the participants who was invited. He's making it seem as if it had been some sort of my own council, which is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Misleading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't speak yet. If the witness is not in a position to answer the question, Mr. Milosevic, my assessment is that he's well placed to say so. Yes, Mr. Primakov.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understand, I can be subjected to cross-examination only within the scope of the examination-in-chief, and questions can also be asked arising out of my answers. However, if some completely extraneous topics are being introduced, I would appreciate it if you would take the same approach as you did in the examination-in-chief when you prevented us from straying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, does this arise out of the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, certainly, yes. And, Your Honour, my only -- my only cautious observation would be if the accused and the witness consume time with procedural matters, the timetable for the witness's return may become problematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, this council -- we can lay it before you in English but I'm afraid not in Russian. This council had a number of contributors, including Dobrica Cosic, this accused, Momir Bulatovic, and others that I've named. Its provenance has not been challenged. Indeed, it was produced by a witness, Zoran Lilic, and there's never been any doubt but that it is a genuine stenographic record of the meeting held on the day Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond following your encounter with this accused. And because my screen isn't working so I'll have to read it out. I'll just get another copy and get my screen repaired at the break. The accused said this, and it can be found Exhibit 469, tab 40, page 73, in the bottom, of 1167. And I'll read it slowly, Mr. Primakov. The accused interrupted, saying, "... there has to be integrity of the Serbian people. We de facto have that because objectively and according to all our relations, such as political, military, economy, cultural, and educational, we have that integrity. The question is how to get the recognition of the unity now, actually how to legalise that unity. How to turn the situation, which de facto exists and could not be de facto endangered into being de facto and de jure? Accordingly, the road, which would lead us to de jure, leads through a 'small labyrinth.' We would never allow the change in a de facto situation, but through that 'small labyrinth' we would achieve some things, if not in half a year, then in a year, if not in a year, then in two years. What do we gain? We gain that we would have fewer casualties and in that way we would save our people. We have to sacrifice everything for the people except the people itself." Now, it will be, of course, Mr. Primakov, for the learned Judges to interpret, as and if necessary, observations and statements by parties such as the accused. If that passage shows the accused planning to turn the de facto position on the ground into a de jure position in a year or so to come, is that something he mentioned to you in your meeting where you discussed Greater Serbia or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be in order for me to get that paper from which Mr. Nice is just quoting. And what he's quoting, even though he's taking it out of context, obviously reflects my advocation of negotiations rather than the war option.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 469, tab 40. It's been referred to twice before at least. The accused has had opportunities with earlier witnesses to deal with context had he so chosen. I return to my question, if I may, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, I'm sorry you were interrupted by the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have 35 tabs here in what I received from Mr. Nice and I don't see tab 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, do you have an additional copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can lay it on the overhead projector --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can lay it on the overhead projector in the English version at the moment and for others to view, while I view it on Ms. Dicklich's monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see what the quotation from this document has to do with my testimony as a witness here. I did not attend these sessions that you seem to be so well-informed about, Mr. Nice, and I don't see why I have to listen to some sort of argument by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... question. The question was whether -- if the passage that was referred to related to a Greater Serbia, was that something which Mr. Milosevic spoke to you about in his meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is an emphatic no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on to something else. From your intelligence-gathering sources or otherwise, were you aware of how the Serb military forces in both Croatia and in Bosnia were paid for?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: What do you mean by "paid for"? You mean the salary they received, or do you mean some additional funds they received? And from whom, then? Would you please specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... asking you the questions, but you're quite --

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're entitled to a clarification and I'm going to give it to you. Were you aware of how officers in the Serb forces operating in Croatia at this time, or the Serb forces operating in Bosnia at this time, were paid for? Who paid them?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I never knew that. I never dealt with that issue in my earlier testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, in all your contacts with the accused, did he ever reveal to you anything about things called the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres by which funding of those forces in respectively Bosnia and Croatia was dealt with?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I never had any such discussion with the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You spoke of the embargo, and you've explained your memory, but let me just help you with one thing. The Vance-Owen Plan failed because the Bosnian Serbs declined. How long was it before an embargo was imposed by the accused? You've said it was in 1993, but think back, please.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Please specify. What are you asking me actually? Are you asking me about 1993?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I'm asking you when you say the arms embargo -- the embargo, I beg your pardon, took effect. Was it in 1993 or was it later?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: The arms embargo was discussed by the Contact Group in 1997, and now you seem to be asking me about the events of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The embargo that the accused applied. I'll try and find your answer on the point because you'd like me to be accurate in what I put to you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This will be the last question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The embargo of the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, against the Republika Srpska, and you told us -- I'm afraid I can't find it now in my notes, but it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: You mean the arms embargo, I can assist you, Mr. Nice. It wasn't an embargo on arms supplies. It was when the parliament of Republika Srpska, Skupstina [phoen], as it was called, of the Republika Srpska declined to ratify the Vance-Owen initiative, then Serbia reacted to this rejection by announcing an embargo allowing only humanitarian aid deliveries, and Serbia qualified the decision of the Republika Srpska parliament as lacking responsibility. You seem to be confused, Mr. Nice. The arms embargo came much later, and it applied to all of Yugoslavia, as decided by the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think what the -- I am aware this may be the last question, but I think the term you used, as I wrote it down, was "economic blockade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is at the bottom part of page 8 in the electronic version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Fine. I can return to that. Let me just get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are going to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you -- perhaps you could check on that during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take a break now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, just to conclude what I was asking you, you spoke of an embargo, as you first described it, an economic blockade. You said it happened in 1993. You're wrong; it happened in the middle of 1994. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: The main point for me was to reiterate that this happened after Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the time when the Assembly of Republika Srpska declined to accept the Vance-Owen Plan, and I wanted to stress that Belgrade reacted to their failure to adopt this plan. This is why I called it the reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But what you didn't explain to the Judges, perhaps because you forgot the date, was that they didn't react for over a year. Now, from everything that you were told by the accused, what could justify them delaying the reaction for over a year?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you're wrong. This was immediately, immediately after that occasion when the parliament of Republika Srpska declined to accept the Vance-Owen Plan, and you seem to be counting the time from that moment when Mr. Milosevic was in Geneva and discussed the plan together with others, or approved the plan together with others. This action, this blockade should not be linked to that date, to that occasion but, rather, to the occasion when the Assembly of Republika Srpska failed to approve that plan, and that was the reaction of Belgrade to that failure to adopt the plan. I used that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, I think your response has been sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. Primakov, if we are to get you on your aeroplane, I'm going to have to ask you to be briefer. But in fact, just to remind you, the embargo or blockade of which you speak occurred on the 4th -- or was announced on the 4th of August, 1994, and it occurred simply because of the failure of a later plan called the Contact Group plan.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is not appropriate for Mr. Nice to keep threatening the witness and telling him that unless his answers are brief, he'll miss his plane. Mr. Nice intervened during my examination numerous times, and all of that was counted against my time. Therefore, I think that this is ridiculous that he keeps repeating for the fifth time to this witness that he'll miss his plane unless he's brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think -- I wouldn't like to think that Mr. Nice intended that. I don't think that was the intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely not. And the Court will understand, the witness will understand, and the accused will understand that we had no knowledge, in light of the three- or four-line 65 ter summary, of the amount of detail that this witness would be dealing with. I'm going to try and finish him in time for him to be free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, as an experienced politician and indeed one spoken of well, as we will subsequently see, by your president, President Yeltsin, you will accept that people, other politicians, may say one thing to one person and another to another. They may keep their plans hidden; correct?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Do you want to use me here as a witness with respect to the conversations that, according to you, Mr. Milosevic had with other people? Because if you want to do that, then this is beyond what I am about to testify here before the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm only going to ask questions once of this witness. Exhibit 469, tab 20, Mr. Primakov, is a record of -- a stenographic record of the Supreme Defence Council of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and in answer to your earlier general question, it was a document provided by the federal authorities direct to this Court in answer to an order. Parts of these documents have been marked not for public use and parts are available for public use. The particular document that I'm looking at has the accused saying one thing on page 11. I'm not going to put it on the overhead projector for reasons of time. But it has the accused saying, and this, for your assistance, is on the 25th of August of 1995, a year after the blockade was announced, that the blockade was merely a formality and that aid flowed daily. In his own words, using your term "blockade," as it happens. He never told you that, did he, that the blockade was just a formality?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Never. The accused, Mr. Milosevic, never told me that this was a mere formality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: As for the document that you're quoting, Mr. Nice, then I would kindly ask that I be allowed to familiarise myself with the document, because I cannot give you an answer after hearing what you're quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's another document that's in evidence. It's a record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just let me deal with that point. Mr. Primakov, are you saying that in order to answer the question, you desire to see the document that Mr. Nice quoted from, which is an exhibit in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me, Your Honour, that my book, the one that was quoted here, was not tendered into evidence, and I think that this is a deviation from the established practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is not so at all. Mr. Nice has tendered into evidence two sections of the book, Exhibit 794, tabs 1 and 2. I'm asking whether, in light of your earlier statement, whether you want to see the exhibit from which he quoted. It's an exhibit in this case and, of course, quite available to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm not interested in that as I've already given my answer. And as I said, I never heard Mr. Milosevic utter the words that Mr. Nice just read out here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We established earlier your close intelligence links and, therefore, trust with the former -- with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia through the accused. Notwithstanding that closeness and trust, he never said anything to you about the reality of the blockade, did he?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I will repeat once again, Mr. Nice, that I never discussed with Mr. Milosevic the fact that this blockade was just a fiction on the part of Yugoslavia. I never heard him utter those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The questions of Mr. Nice distort the facts. It is absolutely impossible for Mr. Primakov to make any other conclusions, because Mr. Primakov knows very well that even the International Monitoring Mission was deployed on the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia headed by Swedish General Bob Pellnas. And even when he's giving the dates, Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have to stop you. You're making a comment, which is inappropriate at this time. Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another exhibit in this case, Mr. Primakov, is a tape recorded -- or a transcript of a tape recording of the 50th National Assembly held under the chairmanship of President Momcilo Krajisnik on the 15th and 16th of April, 1995, in Sanski Most, where the transcript of the tape recording has General Mladic giving an account of the contribution that he had received from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for the war effort until the 31st of December, 1994, which is half a year into the blockade, explaining that he got at least 50 per cent and setting out the tonnes of infantry equipment and matters of that sort. With your intelligence, were you aware of the degree of aid that Mladic was receiving from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Were you, Mr. Primakov?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: We definitely knew about the contacts that were made with General Mladic, but as for the military aid specifically, I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when you say you knew of the contacts, can you tell us, please, what methods -- or by what methods you knew of the contact with Mladic.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I not an accused here and, therefore, I do not have to disclose the methods used by intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe not, but you agreed to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, which doesn't make it for you to be selective. I asked you, please, if you'll tell us by what means you knew of the contact with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I can repeat what I've already said, Mr. Nice. I don't think that this represents a violation of my oath to speak the truth and nothing but the truth. It is not that you're asking me to confirm a fact. You are asking me to tell you through what sources I received that confirmation, and this goes beyond my obligation to speak the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, the investigation into this -- into this accused is without partiality or loyalty by this Prosecution to any country. Our duty is to be dispassionate and to obtain the best evidence that we can. You told us you knew of the contacts between Belgrade, this accused, and Mr. -- and General Mladic. Could you please tell us what material exists so that we can find it, if it's available, and make it available to this Court.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: All I can do is confirm a fact that is widely known to everyone, namely, that Mr. Mladic was not in isolation. However, I cannot give you any specific facts confirming that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've tried it three times, and it will be a matter for argument in due course as to the value of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, did you follow the accused's appearance at the court in Belgrade where he explained that as regards resources spent - this is when he was in custody in Belgrade - as regards resources spent for weapons, ammunition, and other needs of the army of Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina, these expenditures constituted a state secret, and because of state secrets could not be indicated in the law of the budget. He went on to say other things of a like kind, but did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I did not follow Mr. Milosevic's appearance in that trial; therefore, I cannot say anything about what he had stated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Primakov, as is quite clear, and we'll see this from the Contact Group documents when I get to them, as soon as I can, Russia was, to some degree, an ally of this accused, and it appears from your answers that this accused didn't keep you informed with the full truth, did he?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to say that Russia never considered itself an ally of Mr. Milosevic. We took a certain position which stemmed not from what was dictated to us by Mr. Milosevic but, rather, from our understanding and interpretation of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which was to a significant degree dependent on what the accused told you.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: That depended not only on what the accused said to us, although personal conversations and personal relations with Mr. Milosevic were important, but we also took into account the general understanding of the situation in the world and our interpretation of what was going on in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand I didn't mention the Sanski Most exhibit number. It was Exhibit 427, tab 54. We have a bundle of binder -- of documents for the Court. Can I explain it? It covers -- right. I'm grateful. The passage I read out about what the accused said at the Belgrade court is Exhibit 427, tab 3. The documents which we have put in a binder include many documents that have already been produced in evidence. However, it seemed that it would be convenient with this witness to have available a chronological list or chronological connection of documents and so the index that will come to you has many of the items shaded out, and they are documents that have been produced already, and indeed the index shows their reference number. I would ask that all the remaining exhibits be produced as part of this single exhibit, and it will be for the Chamber to decide in due course whether it wishes then to remove and return the exhibits already produced or whether it's happy to leave them in this single binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Many but not all of the documents are Russian, Mr. Primakov, and they all concern, or nearly all concern, the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, while looking at these documents, the Chamber may be assisted by having to hand the second part of the extract from the witness's book, tab 2 of 794. And if the Chamber would be good enough to take that, and if the witness would be good enough to have before him the Russian version of 794, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The excerpts from my book quoted by Mr. Nice, somebody took them from my table. I don't have them in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could be good enough, Mr. Primakov, literally to go to the first paragraph of the Russian version of 794, tab 2, we see that the chapter headed "Target Kosovo" begins: "In 1996, I said to President Slobodan Milosevic: 'Pay attention to Kosovo! An explosive situation is building up there and it will be difficult to deal with it.' I was certain that I was not alone in this conclusion. Many people warned the Serbian President of the potential threat posed by Kosovo." What was his response to your warning?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: His response was as follows: We should not dramatise the situation. I believe that that response was conditioned by the fact that after Dayton, Mr. Milosevic had an impression that the West has changed its attitude with respect to him. His contacts with the West were such that he wasn't disposed to pay attention to this or that acute problem inside the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you go, please, to page 341 in the Russian, and in the English version, at the foot of page 5. In a general narrative part of the history, you said this: "However, the West's attitude to what was happening in Kosovo gradually started to change. Initially the role of first violin was played by Germany, truly alarmed at the fast increase in the number of Albanians emigrants, including those from Kosovo, where armed conflicts became more frequent, and because the Albanian soldiers hid in their villages, the civilian population began to suffer too. The conduct of the Serbian police too was not the most intelligent, with a series of incidents of 'cleansing the terrain'." Of course, you weren't there in person, Mr. Primakov, but what was your understanding of the Serbian police "cleansing the terrain"?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I said during my testimony everything that is in complete harmony with this excerpt from my book. I've already said that to you. Therefore, I don't see, Mr. Nice, why are you quoting this again. I never once deviated from the position expressed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, I must call you to order. The answer is legitimate and proper -- the question is quite proper. Answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question. I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you mean in your book by the phrase "cleansing the terrain"?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: What I had in mind is the following: Based on our assessment, the Kosovo Liberation Army, which was based in Albanian settlements, attacked Serbian settlements and then went back to their bases in Albanian settlements. This is what I told you about. And then at the time, they started an operation in order to expel the KLA from those Albanian settlements. Frequently this took the form of cleansing the terrain, and in the process of these operations, civilians from both ethnic groups suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And civilians of Albanian ethnicity were moved out; correct?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I did not mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm asking you that as a question.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I have no detailed information concerning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will find the picking up of the chronology of Contact Group meetings at the foot of page 6. I probably shan't refer to many pages, and I'll just go through the documents in the binder. For the assistance of the witness, I will summarise many of the documents that we've seen already and probably not take him through them - there simply isn't time - but I shall want his comment on documents that we have yet to look at or have had yet to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Primakov, the exercise is one where I'm reminding you of an overall chronology of reporting. Do you follow? And I shall be asking for your comments on particular passages. If we look, then, at tab 1, we see the statement of the 24th of September, 1997, and we see on tab 2 a further statement of January the 8th, 1998 - give me one minute, please - all of which we've already seen, but I'm taking you to them.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Your Honour, both of these statements are presented to me here in English, and I'm asked to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're not being asked to comment at the moment. I'm simply showing you what's available.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Please tell me, is it reasonable to expect me to do this, to read several pages in English and then to give my comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what is the question? Are you asking --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I'm just reminding him and you of all the documents that exist, and we'll come to the new ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to tab 3, there's a document of the 25th of February, which we have looked at, but I just want you to confirm the evenhandedness of the approach of the Contact Group where we see, and Your Honours will see this four paragraphs down, that the Contact Group meeting is quoted as recording this: "The Contact Group reiterated that it supported neither independence nor the maintenance of the status quo. The principles of the solution of the Kosovo problem should be based on the territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, taking into account the rights of the Kosovo Albanians and all those who live in Kosovo in accordance with OSCE standards, Helsinki principles, and the UN Charter." You would be entirely happy with that part of the statement, correct?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Yes. I'm entirely happy, and I've already mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We come to number 4, tab 4, which the Chamber has already looked at with another witness. It's the document of the 12th of March recording the meeting on the 9th of March. And just to remind you that -- this is in Russian, but I can simply remind you that this is where the Russian Federation declined to support measures about visas and government-financed export credit and matters of that sort. Do you remember that meeting and at that statement? I don't desire any further comment, but it is in Russian for you at the end of the tab.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what paragraph you're referring to and I'll read it out in Russian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. The paragraph which refers to the Russian Federation reservation can be found on, I think, page 4. Let's check that. Yes. After subparagraph (d), where it says that the Contact Group notes that subparagraph (c) and (d) above are not adopted by the Russian Federation.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I can read here that there was a point when the Contact Group noted that the Russian Federation was unable to support proposals regarding immediate imposition of measures (c) and (d), namely, the moratorium on government-financed export credit support for trade and investment as well as denial of visas for senior Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbian representatives. You put a full stop here but I would like to read on, Mr. Nice. It says, nevertheless, if there is no progress in making the steps to which the Contact Group is appealing, then the Russian Federation will be willing to discuss all the above measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: That is the end of that paragraph, and I can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then come to the 25th of March meeting, which is at tab 5, 27th of March, and referring to a meeting on the 25th of March. At this time, you were still in the cabinet of President Yeltsin, although he fired a number of your other cabinet colleagues, I think.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, 1998. If that's the period you are talking about, I was foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you explained, I think, to Madeleine Albright, according to her book, which I haven't copied but just checking whether you agree with this, you confirmed to her that you'd been an ally of President Yeltsin for a long time and he didn't regard you as a potential rival and that's why you'd kept your position.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Well, no. You see, Your Honours, this is going far beyond the scope of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But more interesting, and I want your comment on this, is that Mrs. Albright suggests that by this stage, Russia's particular concern to keep Kosovo as a Serbian problem reflected its own concerns with the possibility of external intervention for Chechnya. Now, that's her view. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I don't see any link between Kosovo and Chechnya in that respect. There could be another link, namely, the terrorist groups that were active in Kosovo were also linked to Chechen terrorists, and that was proved later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 5, then, the record of the 25th of March meeting we've looked at, but I would like you to look at literally the last four lines in the Russian text, and the last four lines, of course, in the English text. This record of the contact groups ends this way: We are basing the principles for a solution on territorial integrity. It goes on to say: "Such a solution must also take into account the rights of the Kosovar Albanians and all those who live in Kosovo. We support a substantially greater degree of autonomy for Kosovo which must include meaningful self-administration." That was a view which you signed up to, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Indisputably, and I still believe it was a proper, correct position. On the one hand, we recognised that Kosovo can only exist within the framework of Yugoslavia, and you are emphasising that yourself by quoting this document. And on the other hand, there was a need to expand Kosovo's autonomy within Yugoslavia. That was Russia's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document 6, please, is a new document. It's a resolution of the Security Council dated the 31st of March. There's a Russian version for you. We notice on the first stage in either version under the heading "Condemning," that the Security Council "condemning the use of excessive force by Serbian police forces against civilians and peaceful demonstrators in Kosovo, as well as all acts of terrorism by the Kosovo Liberation Army or any other group or individual and all external support for terrorist activity in Kosovo, including finance, arms, and training." You, therefore, signed up or agreed to condemnation of excessive force by Serbian police forces at that time, because you were aware of such excessive force. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that this document was not provided for me in Russian. It is rather a fact that Russian is an official language of the United Nations, and all the United Nations documents are issued in Russian, among other languages. As for the excerpt you quoted, yes, we really believed that. And it is emphasised here that terrorists such as the Kosovo Liberation Army are conducting terrorist activities. And on the other hand, the Serbian forces were using excessive force resulting in civilian casualties. I don't see what the issue is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Primakov, if you go to the bottom of your page. And if the Chamber would turn over to the second page. And incidentally, Mr. Primakov, the Russian version has indeed been taken from the United Nations available materials in order to assist you, and I hope you find it useful. We now see that the resolution calls upon the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia immediately to take further necessary steps to achieve a political solution to the issue of Kosovo through dialogue, to implement actions indicated in the Contact Group's earlier statements, calls upon Albanian leaders to condemn terrorist action, emphasises that all elements in the Kosovo Albanian community should pursue their goals by peaceful means. And then at number 5, for example, agrees with particular proposals of the Contact Group about the solution, and we can see those set out. And then at number 9, "decides that all states shall, for the purpose of fostering peace and stability in Kosovo, prevent the sale or supply to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including Kosovo, by their nationals or from territories or using their flag vessels and aircraft, of arms and related materiel ..." We can look at this in more detail later, but at this stage are you happy with the product of the Contact Group's work as reflected in the resolution of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: At that moment, if we had not been happy with the substance of the documents, we would not have signed them. Russia signed them because they reflected the Russian position. So I don't understand the point of your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 7, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say, Mr. Nice, I'm finding it difficult to understand the point of these questions as well when the answers are obvious before the questions are asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is that we saw with a number of these documents with the previous witness that Russia's presence at the Contact Group, as well as, of course, its representation at the United Nations, didn't stop a series of documents developing recording violence on the ground in a way different from the overall thrust of this witness and indeed the last witness's evidence. Now, I'm quite happy to abbreviate matters because I think these documents can be taken more swiftly if you're happy for me to do it in this way, on the basis that these are documents to which this witness and his Russian colleagues signed up, because they will then prove a useful resource for the Chamber as one of a number of resources in assessing what was actually happening. I'm taking him in the new documents to passages that deal either in a particularly evenhanded way with violence by both sides or that are reflective of violence by the Serb side. That's all. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But one question of Mr. Primakov about whether he accepts that these various documents reflect the position held by Russia at the time would have got you to the situation far more --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that if he's prepared to go through the documents with me and just accept that in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, you've seen so far reports and Security Council resolutions, and what there is before the Judges at the moment is a large number of these covering the whole history of the Contact Group and the resolutions that followed from its reports. You've gone through several of these in your evidence, and they're covered in your book, which is available for the Judges. Are there any of them with which you particularly -- with which you know you disagree or are you happy for them to be before the Judges for the reasons I've given, as a report of a position taken by the Contact Group and the United Nations of which Russia was a part?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I think that all these documents have to be evaluated taking into account the time when they were adopted. I cannot evaluate them otherwise. There were certain specific circumstances on the ground in existence, and if these documents are signed by Russia, then they had the Russian support. They had it at the time. We don't even interpret those documents and resolutions that we didn't completely agree with, but there was a core to these documents that we were happy with because we thought it would help stabilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that event, I'll take them a little more swiftly, if I may, but can I take you, please, to tab 9. No Russian for this one, I'm afraid, but you may, I think, remember it and indeed I think it's covered in a chapter in your book.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Mr. Primakov actually said, "We didn't torpedo these documents because there was a core to them we believed was right."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The document which you're looking at, which is, I'm afraid, in English, is a letter of the 17th of June of 1998, from the premanent representative -- well, no. That's from Mr. Lavrov. But if we look at the annex on the following page, we see the joint statement by the president of the Russian Federation and by this accused, President Slobodan Milosevic, as he was, which reflects the accused's joint position at that time to resolve, and if we look at it in summary in the bulleted points, "to resolve by political means the problem." And then two bullet points down, "to refrain from taking any repressive measures against peaceful populations." And then towards the bottom of the page, the last bullet point but one, "to allow the free return of all refugees and displaced persons on the basis of programmes agreed," and then it says in the last bullet point, "to the extent that terrorist activities are halted, to reduce the presence of security forces outside the areas in which they are permanently deployed." So this is in the summer of 1998. Did you yourself accept on the evidence available to you that there was need for the Yugoslav president, in this public statement, to say that he would refrain from taking repressive measures against peaceful populations?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: You quoted a joint statement that I already mentioned earlier in my testimony. It was a document developed during Mr. Milosevic's visit to Moscow, and it was signed by two presidents; President Yeltsin and President Milosevic. The text of the document that you quoted from, from the English version, if I understand, you quoted correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document that that we haven't looked at is number 11. I'll just look at number 10 for a minute, if I may. No, there's nothing on 10. Your Honours, 11 is a report. It's part of the chronology of documents and it's there for completeness, but I needn't refer to it. Number 12 we've already looked at and there's nothing I wish to say about that. Number 13 is a new one. It's a further report in the sequence. There are a number of passages I could take you to which set out allegations of continuing violence, I think on both sides, and it's part of the continuing picture. But in light of the witness's answer that he's already given, they're compendiously produced. Likewise number 14, which is a report of the Secretary-General. Again, I needn't take you to detail of it, but it continues the story. Perhaps we will just look at this one, because it provides snapshot pictures of where we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look at number 14, please, Mr. Primakov, which is the 4th of September, 1998, and is a report to the Secretary-General -- report of the Secretary-General. And if you'd be good enough, please, to go to numbered paragraph 7 under "Humanitarian concerns." The record that was made by this stage was of 600 to 700 civilians having been killed in the fighting in Kosovo since March with an estimated cumulative displacement of over 230.000 people. And then at paragraph 8, it says: "According to the UNHCR estimates, there could be up to 50.000 displaced people in Kosovo who have been forced from their homes into the woods and mountains." Are those figures that you were able then and are you able now to accept?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I simply don't know. If that's the report of the secretary-general, and if he's quoting some figures, then they must be based on the information that was available to him. But the question of whether I agree with each of these figures or not is out of place, because it is absolutely not within my competence as a witness to confirm or not to confirm something that is said by the secretary-general in his own report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can do no more than ask that question, Your Honour, and I'm going to move on. We can see in the index or the document that 16 is the report of -- sorry, 16 is not produced. 17 is the Verification Mission agreement which you've already had produced to you. 18 is the agreement on the OSCE Verification Mission. 19 is a new Resolution. We're now at the 24th of October. And this is the one that establishes the Kosovo Verification Mission. I'm not going to go through, I think, probably any of these in details, but you can see a number of findings or various headings on the second page of that, number 19. 20 and 21 we've had in already. 22 is a further report of the 12th of November. Nothing particular that I need to refer to. Number 23, Christmas Eve 1998, or 24th of December, 1998, with a report on this day, as you will see, Mr. Primakov, at the end of the first page in your version, paragraph 4, that the secretary-general was obliged to report that no significant improvement and alarming signs of potential deterioration while sources report that the cease-fire is holding there are indications of tension on the ground. And he goes on to say that violence has reached its highest level since the 16th of October agreement, 50 persons having died in violent attacks. And there's more comment on that later. Do you accept that there was this sign of an increase in violence at this time by December 1998?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: There was a lot of varying information, and I would like to point out one more thing in that report of the Secretary-General where he says that there is no new information about kidnappings from mid-September. In the same place in the report, you see support expressed to the cease-fire. That is one among other indicators showing that there was a different trend going on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 24 we've already seen, and 25, which I don't need to add to. 26 is a further report of the 30th of January of 1999. It deals with the Racak massacre. The witness hasn't, I think, volunteered anything particular about Racak, and unless there's anything he wants to add to what his evidence is, on Racak, we'll move on to tab 27. Tab 27 I would like to trouble you with, please, Mr. Primakov. I'm afraid it's, I think, only in English. It's an existing exhibit. It's a letter by Serbia's head of delegation, Ratko Markovic, to Hill -- to Ambassadors Hill, Petritsch, and Maiorsky, the Russian ambassador. And at this time in negotiations at Rambouillet: "The delegation of the Republic of Serbia wishes to emphasise that major progress has been achieved in the talks at Rambouillet in defining political solution on substantial self-government of Kosovo and Metohija respectful of sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. "We would particularly like to emphasise, the same as the Contact Group, that there can be no independence of Kosovo and Metohija, nor the third republic. "Therefore, all elements of self-government at the time of defining of the agreement have to be known and clearly defined. In further work, this should be adequately addressed and consistently resolved. And in that sense, we are ready to participate in the next meeting on the issue. "The FRY agreed to discuss the scope and character of the international presence in Kosmet to implement the agreement to be accepted in Rambouillet. "The FRY of Yugoslavia -- the FR of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia are fully ready to continue the work in line with the positive spirit of this meeting. We therefore consider it would be extremely useful to set a reasonable deadline to create appropriate conditions and different approach to successfully resume the work and address those questions." Now -- I'd like to point out that direct talks between the two delegations would be useful. The evidence before the court includes, from Mr. Petritsch, that it was at this date, on the 23rd of February, that things suddenly changed. We can see, if you -- and that's why I've read it in full, that Ratko Markovic is positive about the prospects for a solution. The evidence may be - it's entirely for the Court to decide - that it was the accused who at this time, the 23rd of February or thereabouts, reversed the decision and made Rambouillet an impossibility. Can you help the Judges, please, with why it was that the accused from this moment on, if that's the case, was not willing to agree?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I should like to say, Mr. Nice, that a book, a compilation of interviews, was published in Italy, interviews given by Prime Minister Dini of Italy, where he speaks about Rambouillet, saying that there was no agreement because the word "military" was added to the words "international presence." Mr. Dini says in his interview that if another compromise word had been found, it would have been possible to get out of that impasse if the other side had withdrawn that word "military international presence." And my opinion happens to coincide with the opinion of Mr. Dini.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So just that one word would have led to a complete refusal by this accused. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: The point is not in the semantics or in one word alone but what is behind that word, namely, acceptance or failure to accept, unwillingness to accept the military presence of NATO in Kosovo on a permanent or temporary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We move on from that. Thank you for the explanation. 28 and 29 we've seen. 30 is a new report of the 17th of March of 1999. I needn't trouble the Court with any detail of that. 31 is the letter from Zoran Lilic. Do you -- and it's been put in because it fits in chronologically at this place, although it is an existing exhibit. Are you familiar with the letter that Zoran Lilic wrote to the accused?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Well, I see here certain -- your Deputy Prime Minister Zoran Lilic. Is this right? I don't even know this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Move on. 32 is a further letter with an annex, a statement by the chairman on the conclusion of the G8 foreign ministers at the Petersberg centre. Are you acquainted with this statement? It's also in Russian.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: It's a Security Council document. Am I right, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: It is a statement by the chairman on the conclusion of the meeting of the ministers of foreign affairs of the G8 at the Petersberg centre. At that time I was no longer minister of foreign affairs and thus I did not participate in that meeting. Hence I cannot be familiarised with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order to maximise the use of the witness's time and not to inconvenience him, can we deal with how to exhibit this bundle of documents later, perhaps after he has withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few other matters, Mr. Primakov, in light of the answers that you've given. You've suggested that the Western media was in some way orchestrated in a way hostile to Serbia, and you suggested -- in your evidence, you suggested that this went right back to the beginning or certainly the middle of the 1990s. Can you explain by what mechanism the whole of the Western -- not the whole of but a substantial part of the Western press is being orchestrated to advance an anti-Serbian line?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I would like you to quote me correctly, Mr. Nice. I did not say that the Western press initiated, as you just claim, any armed clashes. I said that the Western press had an unbalanced approach to these events by promoting anti-Serb moves. And I said that, and I continue to say that, because I personally witnessed a number of such TV broadcasts in this light.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's in light of your observation, which I recorded in my handwritten notes, as the attitude of the Western media, the whole attitude of the Western media. As you know, the Western media likes to think of itself as free, so I want you to help us, if you can, with why, on your account, the Western media generally should be reporting falsely in a way that's unfavourable to Serbia. Because this isn't a controlled press, this is a free press.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: So you would like to say that it is not possible to have any biased approaches in the Western press in their overview of any events. I cannot agree to such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your observation about the number of refugees in Germany is something that's no doubt based on intelligence coming to you, and it's right, isn't it, that by the middle of the 1990s and the late 1990s, a very large number of Kosovo Albanians had fled Kosovo to go to live in Germany. You were able to make the point at the window that if your colleague went and took the names of the demonstrators they'd all run away because they wouldn't want to go back. What was driving them out, Mr. Primakov? What was driving the Kosovo Albanians out of Kosovo, on your information?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Those were not even closed information sources. This is something I heard directly by Foreign Minister Kinkel, that many came to that country, and they started working in that country, and undoubtedly, according to him, an Albanian community was being shaped which -- and 3 per cent of all the salaries have to be transferred to the KLA supporters and they're forced to do so. It would be very difficult to do that because they all live in a single community, and this would be very difficult to deal with because this creates a big problem for Germany, according to him. And he told me directly that he would be advocating the idea of having those people go back, and he told me directly. At the same time, unfortunately, even after having in Kosovo an Albanian influence being established there - and nobody can deny this - they do not rush back, many of them do not rush back to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, you've painted a picture of Kosovo Liberation Army being the offenders save to the limited extent you allow them to have been retaliating in an excessive way. Isn't the reality also that throughout the 1990s, and particularly towards the end of the 1990s, on information coming to you, Kosovo Albanians were being driven out by violence and by interference with their human rights at the hands of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I believe that there were such instances, just like currently we have the mass exodus of Serbs from Kosovo because of the violation of their rights. At the same time, I would like to reiterate once again that, according to our data, the greatest wave of immigrants started to take place after the commencement of shellings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I wanted to ask you about that. You say they -- the greatest wave started after the commencement of shellings. You will recognise that that doesn't mean that they started because of the shellings. You may not have been following the evidence in this court, but there's been a great deal of evidence of a pattern of driving Kosovo Albanians out. Killing some, driving the rest out. And then at the borders, or sometimes on the way to the borders, depriving them, in a routine way, of their documents of identification. All of these are matters, of course, for the Judges to decide as facts, but dealing with that last point, the systematic removal of people's documents of identification, can you explain that from the information coming to you at all?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you just quoted from the documents of the United Nations organisation and the Contact Group, from which it can be derived that indeed during the military operations which took place there, there were some violations from both parties, and I wouldn't like to represent the picture in one way, pattern. Indeed, what happened, there was a mass evacuation, it took place during the bombings, and I would like to reiterate that once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would like to give you a chance to answer the question and I'll move on. If the Judges in due course find this to be a matter of fact, something that happened, can you give any explanation for the systematic removal and indeed destruction of documents of identification by the Kosovo Albanians driven from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Once again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice says that it is up to the Chamber to decide, and then he's putting a question to the witness as though this fact had been proven. I can't turn my microphone on. It is on now. You know that I cannot activate my microphone by myself. You are in charge of that. Namely, Mr. Robinson, Mr. Nice said that it was up to the Chamber to determine that, and then he puts a question to Mr. Primakov about some systematic confiscation of documents, presenting it as an established fact. I don't think this is proper. I don't think he can present it as an established fact, because here, among a number of these false witnesses there were a number of false testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Firstly, Mr. Milosevic -- firstly, it's proper to explore issues of fact as distinct from law. Secondly, Mr. Nice, I agree with Mr. Milosevic; you should not have put the question in that way. It assumes that the witness agreed that there was a systematic confiscation of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly had no intention to make that assumption. Rather, the reverse. I indeed invited the contrary assumption, said that simply if it happened, did the witness have an explanation? And in my respectful submission, that's not only an appropriate but a potentially very helpful matter to raise because in this particular case, if it is found that there is systematic behaviour, otherwise unexplained, then witnesses who may have knowledge are witnesses who may be able to help us. And I -- I suspect the answer is going to be negative from the witness, but I would press on my liberty to have an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But did you put it -- did you put it in a hypothetical way?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, as I hope I made clear and I hope emerged clearly through the translation, I was asking the question hypothetically, namely: Were it to be the case that there was a systematic taking and destruction of documents of identification of Kosovo Albanians when they - let's use a neutral term - leaving the territory, can you explain from all your knowledge how that happened?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say, Mr. Nice, that I never worked either for the Serb police or in those bodies which were in charge either by the -- by -- who were in charge of taking away those documents are giving the order to do so. The hypothetical nature of your raising this question allows me to categorically state that I know nothing about these facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness has answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In my remaining four or five minutes, just, I think, three things but I will take them slightly out of order in case I can't do all three of them. President Yeltsin is the author of a book called Midnight Diaries in which he sets out what happened following your both becoming Prime Minister and then your ceasing to be Prime Minister before the time when the bombing ceased. And indeed he explains how it was that he dismissed you. But he speaks of a meeting on May the 13th of President Jacques Chirac and how President Chirac made it clear to President Yeltsin that he had to make his mind up whether to support Milosevic or not. Are you aware of that meeting and can you confirm the account, in summary, that President Yeltsin gave in his book?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Mr. Nice sticks to the chronology very nicely. This must be your strong suit. I ceased to be chairman of the government on the 12th of May, and you require me to tell you about the meeting which took place between Milosevic and Chirac on the 13th of May, which is on the next day. On that very day I happened to be at a soccer championship and was watching soccer because I had been freed from the position of chairman of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Throughout his dealings through you and then presumably through Chernomyrdin after you, which brought matters to a conclusion, Yeltsin -- President Yeltsin had a low regard for and didn't want -- well, he had a low regard for the accused; is that correct? Is that your experience?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: You would like to create an image of a witness, reverting to, Your Honour, resorting to impermissible ways, and this is not the reason why I came here. You can refer to the book, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it -- and then finally, was it the understanding in the Russian leadership until the day of your departure, was it the understanding that the accused was gambling on having Russian support for his position and that it was a gamble that didn't pay off?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: I believe that under the harsh conditions which were established in Yugoslavia, nobody was gambling in politics. This has nothing to do with any major Yugoslav politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only one other question of detail: You've referred to the 30th of March meeting that you had with the accused after the bombing started. I don't think it's in the book that we've been looking at. Is it in any other book or can you tell us where we can find it recorded documentally anywhere else? Maybe it's in your book and we've missed it, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Can you, please, since you believe so, that my moderate, yes, literature allows you to better comprehend the situation, I would like recommend you to read another book of mine which obviously is not known to you. It is called Eight Months Plus. In that book, by the way, you can find, as far as I understand, in an objective way all the details of my dismissal of position of the chairman of the government or the Prime Minister. I can tell you that the president of the Russian Federation, President Yeltsin, offered to me to write the statements requesting my dismissal in any language, in any wording. You raised this question, and please do not prevent me from answering it. And I said that this would be his constitutional right, and I would not try to simplify his job. And in that book, you can find a clear-cut description of all my negotiations and discussions with Gore. You can find the minutes of those meetings, you can find my notes, and in that book, you can also find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have stopped you because that's a sufficient plug for your book, the other book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. There were a number of other topics, but I see the time, so I'll stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have questions for re-examination, and I understood I have ten minutes. Just please mind the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Primakov, Mr. Nice asked you at the beginning if you were aware about the Council for Harmonising Stands in State Policy, and he enumerated me, General Mladic, and I don't know who else, and you told him you were not aware of that council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention, for the record and for the sake of this exhibit, that at the beginning of this stenogram, it is set out very clearly who attended. It is said that it was chaired by the president of Yugoslavia, attended by the presidents of Serbia and other republics, the Prime Minister, and certain ministers, and it goes on to say members of the council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm -- I've just stopped you. Is that a document that you're going to tender through this witness? Is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was tendered already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was tendered already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the document introduced by Mr. Nice. He asked questions of this witness based on it. And then Dobrica Cosic, who was the chairman in opening the session, says: "I hereby open the session of the council attended also by representatives by the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear, Mr. Primakov, that we're not talking about members of the council from Republika Srpska and the Serbian Krajina, that they are just invited to attend the session of the council?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: You have given this clarification and I'm inclined to agree with it, but I know nothing about the council itself or the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice presented this document because, as he says, the meeting took place on the 9th of January, after our meeting, in order to show a different stand on my part compared to what I had told you. I will quote here. I have many quotations ready, but I don't have time. But at the very beginning of my participation in the discussion at that meeting, I quote, I said, "It is our strategic aim for the Serbian people in the Balkans to be free and equal. The equality of the Serbian people implies having all the opportunities to assert and protect its interests." And then it goes on to say: "I'm absolutely certain that we haven't used up the entire negotiating room available to us, and it is upon us to use the negotiating space to the maximum with utmost responsibility." So I'm talking to the representatives of all the republics, including the representatives of Republika Srpska and Serbian Krajina, and I'm telling them that we should go to negotiations. Is that completely in line with what I had earlier told you?

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: You spoke about the necessity for a political settlement. I have already spoken about that. As for particular documents or your specific statements, I cannot testify to that because I have no specific knowledge, but what you just said coincides with your viewpoint as expressed to me when we discussed other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 58, I say again regarding settlement in Bosnia-Herzegovina: "It should admit and accept a constitution based on tripartite consensus." I used the word "consensus" here, I used the word "consensus" when talking to you. So is this completely in keeping with what I had told you? I'm talking about tripartite consensus of the three constituent peoples.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: You not only said that to me, but I also quoted your statement for the Belgrade TV when they recorded an interview with you in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Primakov, in conclusion concerning this document, and I will quote again from this document, but I would appreciate it if you could give Mr. Primakov this entire document so he can read it later when he has time just to see how consistent I was speaking in this forum relative to my discussions with him. And I'm quoting again from the stenographic notes. I said we were not a party to the conflict in Bosnia. Serbia is not represented at Geneva negotiations. The Yugoslav delegation is there representing Yugoslav federal institutions. So we, Yugoslavia, as a federation, are represented. It is Lord Owen who insisted, saying, "You cannot refuse to give a contribution." Page 12. He came out in front of cameras and: "On behalf of the European Community, I invited Mr. Milosevic to participate in the work of the Geneva conference, to give his contribution." Was it clear to you then that there are three sides negotiating in Geneva; the Muslim, Croat, and Bosnian Serb sides, whereas I was invited to give a contribution to a peaceful settlement, and you were the one who insisted that I should certainly contribute to that peaceful settlement? That speaks to the nature of my participation in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: That is correct. There were three delegations involved there, and we intensified our discussions with you resulting in your travel to Geneva after it became clear that your presence there could help find a way out of the impasse that had been reached. And in my earlier testimony, I already said that you did precisely that, because on the eve of your arrival, Republika Srpska declined to agree to the constitutional order suggested by the Vance-Owen Plan, and you exerted a very important positive influence. So the Bosnian Serb delegation abandoned their previous position on the very next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since we don't have any more time, just a few more brief questions arising from the cross. Mr. Nice questioned you about the stances expressed in the Contact Group. Tell me, please, were the positions of the Contact Group an expression of unity or an expression of compromise between the Russian members and other members or maybe among various members? So it's unity versus compromise.

utterances.speaker: YEVGENY PRIMAKOV
utterances.text: This is how I should answer this question: In a number of issues, we achieved unity. On certain documents, there was compromise, in order not to lose the positive outcome that this compromise was able to yield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
